=== CALL C0341 ===
Rebecca: Hiya! Oh, there you are. Can you hear me alright?
Agnieszka: Yes. Fine.
Rebecca: Brilliant. I'm Rebecca, I'm in Exeter. Sorry about the state of the kitchen behind me, I've literally just got in.
Agnieszka: Agnieszka. Wakefield.
Rebecca: Wakefield, lovely. I've never been, erm, I've driven past it on the M1, does that count?
Agnieszka: Most people only drive past it. So yes, it counts.
Rebecca: Ha! What do you do then, if you don't mind me asking?
Agnieszka: I teach maths. Secondary school, mostly year 7, 8, 9. Some GCSE.
Rebecca: Oh god, respect. I was terrible at maths. I'm a vet, I sort of, kind of got through the stats module by crying at it, basically.
Agnieszka: Vet with which animals?
Rebecca: Mostly cattle and sheep, out near Crediton. TB testing, calvings, that kind of thing, and then some cats and dogs in the afternoons. And on call, which is why I look knackered. I was up at three with a heifer who did not want to cooperate, you know?
Agnieszka: Three in the morning. And you are still smiling. That is suspicious.
Rebecca: Honestly it's the only way to survive it. You laugh or you, yeah. Do you get the same with year 8s?
Agnieszka: Year 8 on a Friday afternoon is worse than your heifer. Your heifer at least does not have a phone.
Rebecca: Fair. That's very fair. Did you do the puzzle bit at the start, by the way? I got proper stuck on the third one.
Agnieszka: I did it. It was fine. But the instructions were badly written, you know? It said "choose the best answer" and two answers were correct. So either they made a mistake or they are testing if you notice.
Rebecca: See, I didn't even notice that, I just picked one and moved on.
Agnieszka: That is also an answer.
Rebecca: That's basically how I do my clinical notes as well. Get it done, sofa, half ten at night. Don't tell anyone.
Agnieszka: My marking is the same. I am always behind. But the results are good, so nobody says anything.
Rebecca: Right, exactly, results speak. Are you from Wakefield originally? I'm guessing not, from the accent, sorry, is that rude?
Agnieszka: No, it's obvious. I am from Poland, Tarnów, in the south. I came in 2006, Leeds first, then Wakefield. So now I say "tea" for dinner and my sister laughs at me on the phone.
Rebecca: Ha, I say dinner and we eat it at about nine, so I'm no help. Do you get back much?
Agnieszka: Every summer. Two, three weeks. My mother is there.
Rebecca: That's nice. I'm awful at going home, my parents are only in Stroud and I barely see them, which is a bit shameful with the M5 right there.
Agnieszka: It's always easier when it's far. Then you have an excuse.
Rebecca: Yeah, that's true actually. Erm, what do you do to switch off? I'm guessing not sea swimming. I swim at Exmouth most of the year, it's proper cold right now.
Agnieszka: In the sea. Now. In this weather.
Rebecca: Yep. Wetsuit only when it's really bad.
Agnieszka: No. I do sudoku. Crime novels. Warm things, inside, with a blanket.
Rebecca: Honestly that sounds lovely as well, I'm not judging—
Agnieszka: I am judging a little bit. The sea in February is for fish.

=== CALL C0343 ===
Callum: Alright! Can you hear me okay?
Agnieszka: Yes. I can hear you.
Callum: Sound. I'm Callum, I'm in St Helens, near Liverpool, sort of between Liverpool and Wigan. Depends who you ask, to be fair.
Agnieszka: Agnieszka. Wakefield.
Callum: Oh, not far then, over the Pennines. What do you do?
Agnieszka: Maths teacher. Secondary.
Callum: Ah, no way. You look like a maths teacher, I mean that nicely! I had a Mrs Kelly who used to stare at me exactly like that when I hadn't done me homework.
Agnieszka: Had you done it?
Callum: Never, no. Got a C in the end, so she must've been doing something right.
Agnieszka: A C is a pass. She did her job. What do you do?
Callum: I work at the glassworks, on the float line. So erm, basically you've got this massive furnace, and the molten glass comes out and floats on a bath of tin, and it spreads out flat into a ribbon. I'm on the hot end, so I'm watching temperatures, checking the thickness, flagging any defects. It's all shifts, four on, four off, days and nights.
Agnieszka: Glass floats on tin. I didn't know that.
Callum: Yeah, it's mad when you first see it. Tin's heavier, so the glass just sits on top, perfectly flat. That's how you get your windows.
Agnieszka: My husband would have liked that. He was an engineer. He liked anything that is clever and boring at the same time.
Callum: Clever and boring, that's the job description, to be fair. Most nights it's boring, which is how you want it. Boring means nothing's gone wrong.
Agnieszka: Same in a classroom. Boring lesson, nobody is throwing chairs. Good day.
Callum: Ha! Do they throw chairs?
Agnieszka: Year 8 on a Friday, everything is possible.
Callum: Did you do the puzzle bit at the start? I was dead pleased with meself, then I got to the last one and just guessed.
Agnieszka: I did it. One question had two correct answers. Badly written.
Callum: Did it? Which one?
Agnieszka: The one with the shapes, number three. "Choose the best answer." Two were equally good.
Callum: See, that's why you'd want her on your quiz team. I run a pub quiz team on Thursdays, I'm captain. We could do with someone who argues with the quizmaster.
Agnieszka: I would argue with the quizmaster. Often he is wrong.
Callum: He is wrong! Last week he had the Moon landing as '68. Sixty-nine, mate. I've listened to about four podcasts on it.
Agnieszka: Then you were right. Did you get the point?
Callum: No! He wouldn't give it me. Still not over it.
Agnieszka: This is why I do sudoku. Nobody can tell you the answer is wrong when it is right.
Callum: That's fair, that. Erm, what do you do when you're not marking? Are you from Wakefield originally, or...?
Agnieszka: Poland. Tarnów. I came 2006. My son is seventeen, A-levels, he eats everything in the fridge. That is my hobby now, buying food for him.
Callum: Ha, me mum says the exact same about me brother. Is he going uni then?
Agnieszka: He wants to. Engineering, maybe. Like his father.
Callum: Ah, that's nice, that. Honestly I sometimes wish I'd gone. I did an apprenticeship instead, and I've no regrets, like, but I do love learning stuff. I've been looking at the company paying for an HNC, in manufacturing engineering.
Agnieszka: Then do it. If they pay, do it. You will regret it if you don't.
Callum: Yeah. Yeah, me wife says that too.
Agnieszka: Then she is also right. Two people telling you.
Callum: [laughs] Okay, okay, I'll look at the forms on—

=== CALL C0344 ===

Abena: Biomedical science, first year. I'd like to go into haematology, in an NHS lab, hopefully.
Rebecca: Oh, brilliant. Why haematology?

Abena: Oh, that's really cool. Do you do the testing yourself, or does it go to a lab?

Abena: [laughs] Do you have pets as well, or is that too much?
Rebecca: One lurcher, Moss. That's her back end in the corner there. She stole a whole block of cheddar off the counter last week, the entire thing, wrapper and all. Proper criminal.
Abena: Oh no. Was she okay?
Rebecca: She was fine, smug, if anything. Do you have any animals?

Rebecca: That totally counts. What are they called?
Abena: Erm, the monstera's called Gloria. She's just got a new leaf, actually, so I'm quite proud of her.
Rebecca: Gloria! That's amazing. See, you're way better at keeping things alive than me, I killed a sourdough starter. That's literally just flour and water and I couldn't—
Abena: Sorry, go on.
Rebecca: No, no, I was just going to say, Moss probably ate it.

Agnieszka: Thriller. With a detective?
Dominic: Sort of. There's a police officer, but he's useless, which is the point. It's more about this family in one flat, and something's wrong with the neighbour, and you spend two hours not sure who's lying. By the end you don't trust anyone in it, including the kid. It's very tight. Nothing wasted. Every shot's doing a job.
Agnieszka: I like this. I read crime novels, Polish and Scandinavian. And I watch every detective series on the TV. My husband used to say I always know who did it by twenty minutes.
Dominic: Do you?
Agnieszka: Usually. In British dramas, it's the famous actor who is in the first episode for only one scene. Always him.
Dominic: [laughs] Yeah. That's a casting problem. Once you've paid for someone, you have to use them.
Agnieszka: So I am right.
Dominic: You're right. Don't tell anyone in the industry.
Agnieszka: I don't know anyone in the industry. Only you.
Dominic: Then it's safe.
Agnieszka: You go to galleries also? You have this print behind you, the orange.
Dominic: Yeah, a bit. Openings, studios in East London. I haven't hung that one yet.
Agnieszka: In Wakefield we have the Hepworth. I went once when it opened. A lot of concrete.
Dominic: It is a lot of concrete. I've been, actually. The building's alright. Some of the Hepworth pieces are, er, very good.
Agnieszka: Maybe. I looked at the concrete, I looked at the river, I went home.
Dominic: That's a review, to be fair.
Agnieszka: Short reviews are best. Like my marking. "Show working." Done.
Dominic: What's the Polish crime writer I should read? If I was going to start somewhere.
Agnieszka: Somewhere easy, translated. There is one, Miłoszewski, the prosecutor Szacki books. He is miserable, everybody is miserable, it rains. You would like it.
Dominic: Why would I—
Agnieszka: Because you look like you would like miserable people in the rain. I mean it nicely.

calls.C0341:
Rebecca: Hiya! Oh, there you are. Can you hear me alright?
Agnieszka: Yes. Fine.
Rebecca: Brilliant. I'm Rebecca, I'm in Exeter. Sorry about the state of the kitchen behind me, I've literally just got in.
Agnieszka: Agnieszka. Wakefield.
Rebecca: Wakefield, lovely. I've never been, erm, I've driven past it on the M1, does that count?
Agnieszka: Most people only drive past it. So yes, it counts.
Rebecca: Ha! What do you do then, if you don't mind me asking?
Agnieszka: I teach maths. Secondary school, mostly year 7, 8, 9. Some GCSE.
Rebecca: Oh god, respect. I was terrible at maths. I'm a vet, I sort of, kind of got through the stats module by crying at it, basically.
Agnieszka: Vet with which animals?
Rebecca: Mostly cattle and sheep, out near Crediton. TB testing, calvings, that kind of thing, and then some cats and dogs in the afternoons. And on call, which is why I look knackered. I was up at three with a heifer who did not want to cooperate, you know?
Agnieszka: Three in the morning. And you are still smiling. That is suspicious.
Rebecca: Honestly it's the only way to survive it. You laugh or you, yeah. Do you get the same with year 8s?
Agnieszka: Year 8 on a Friday afternoon is worse than your heifer. Your heifer at least does not have a phone.
Rebecca: Fair. That's very fair. Did you do the puzzle bit at the start, by the way? I got proper stuck on the third one.
Agnieszka: I did it. It was fine. But the instructions were badly written, you know? It said "choose the best answer" and two answers were correct. So either they made a mistake or they are testing if you notice.
Rebecca: See, I didn't even notice that, I just picked one and moved on.
Agnieszka: That is also an answer.
Rebecca: That's basically how I do my clinical notes as well. Get it done, sofa, half ten at night. Don't tell anyone.
Agnieszka: My marking is the same. I am always behind. But the results are good, so nobody says anything.
Rebecca: Right, exactly, results speak. Are you from Wakefield originally? I'm guessing not, from the accent, sorry, is that rude?
Agnieszka: No, it's obvious. I am from Poland, Tarnów, in the south. I came in 2006, Leeds first, then Wakefield. So now I say "tea" for dinner and my sister laughs at me on the phone.
Rebecca: Ha, I say dinner and we eat it at about nine, so I'm no help. Do you get back much?
Agnieszka: Every summer. Two, three weeks. My mother is there.
Rebecca: That's nice. I'm awful at going home, my parents are only in Stroud and I barely see them, which is a bit shameful with the M5 right there.
Agnieszka: It's always easier when it's far. Then you have an excuse.
Rebecca: Yeah, that's true actually. Erm, what do you do to switch off? I'm guessing not sea swimming. I swim at Exmouth most of the year, it's proper cold right now.
Agnieszka: In the sea. Now. In this weather.
Rebecca: Yep. Wetsuit only when it's really bad.
Agnieszka: No. I do sudoku. Crime novels. Warm things, inside, with a blanket.
Rebecca: Honestly that sounds lovely as well, I'm not judging—
Agnieszka: I am judging a little bit. The sea in February is for fish.
calls.C0342:
Abena: Oh, hi. Sorry, I wasn't sure if it had started.
Dominic: Yeah, it's on. Hi.
Abena: Hi. Erm, I'm Abena.
Dominic: Dominic.
Abena: Nice to meet you.
Dominic: You too. Where are you?
Abena: Chelmsford. I'm at Anglia Ruskin, first year, doing biomedical science. So, yeah, kind of in the thick of it at the moment.
Dominic: Right. Is that like, lab stuff?
Abena: Yeah, mostly. Like, we do practicals on blood samples and cell cultures and stuff. I'd like to work in an NHS lab eventually, maybe haematology. Sorry, that's probably more than you asked.
Dominic: No, it's fine. That's a proper job. More useful than mine, anyway.
Abena: What do you do?
Dominic: I run a post-production company in Soho. Editing, colour, sound. Mostly adverts, some TV. We did a thing for one of the supermarkets last Christmas, the one with the, er, the fox. So, yeah.
Abena: Oh, I think I've seen that one, actually. With the fox in the snow?
Dominic: That's the one.
Abena: That's really cool. My brother watched it, like, ten times.
Dominic: He's in the minority then. Most people skip adverts.
Abena: [laughs] Do you live in Soho as well, or...?
Dominic: No, Walthamstow. I get the Victoria line in, which was knackered again this morning, so. Forty minutes stood next to someone's rucksack.
Abena: Oh, same, I get the 100 bus to uni and it's never on time. I've kind of given up planning around it. I just leave really early and then I'm sat there for ages.
Dominic: Yeah. That's the sensible way.
Abena: Erm... sorry, I'm not very good at this bit.
Dominic: You're fine. I'm not either really. What do you do when you're not studying?
Abena: I read a lot, mostly. And I draw a bit, like botanical drawings, with fine-liners. That's what's on my wall, behind me.
Dominic: I wondered. They look good. What are you reading?
Abena: Right now I'm rereading The Dispossessed, by Ursula Le Guin? It's sci-fi but it's not really about spaceships, it's more about, like, two worlds that are organised completely differently and this physicist who goes between them and doesn't really belong in either one. I don't know if that makes sense. I just think she makes you look at normal things like they're strange. Sorry, I'm rambling.
Dominic: No, that's... yeah. That's sort of what good films do as well. I saw a Korean thriller at the Prince Charles last week that did that, made a normal flat look like the scariest place in the world.
Abena: Is that a cinema?
Dominic: Yeah, off Leicester Square. Small, bit grubby, best place in London. You should go sometime, if you're ever in.
Abena: Maybe. I mostly just go to Cambridge if I go anywhere. What was the film called?
Dominic: It's, er—
calls.C0343:
Callum: Alright! Can you hear me okay?
Agnieszka: Yes. I can hear you.
Callum: Sound. I'm Callum, I'm in St Helens, near Liverpool, sort of between Liverpool and Wigan. Depends who you ask, to be fair.
Agnieszka: Agnieszka. Wakefield.
Callum: Oh, not far then, over the Pennines. What do you do?
Agnieszka: Maths teacher. Secondary.
Callum: Ah, no way. You look like a maths teacher, I mean that nicely! I had a Mrs Kelly who used to stare at me exactly like that when I hadn't done me homework.
Agnieszka: Had you done it?
Callum: Never, no. Got a C in the end, so she must've been doing something right.
Agnieszka: A C is a pass. She did her job. What do you do?
Callum: I work at the glassworks, on the float line. So erm, basically you've got this massive furnace, and the molten glass comes out and floats on a bath of tin, and it spreads out flat into a ribbon. I'm on the hot end, so I'm watching temperatures, checking the thickness, flagging any defects. It's all shifts, four on, four off, days and nights.
Agnieszka: Glass floats on tin. I didn't know that.
Callum: Yeah, it's mad when you first see it. Tin's heavier, so the glass just sits on top, perfectly flat. That's how you get your windows.
Agnieszka: My husband would have liked that. He was an engineer. He liked anything that is clever and boring at the same time.
Callum: Clever and boring, that's the job description, to be fair. Most nights it's boring, which is how you want it. Boring means nothing's gone wrong.
Agnieszka: Same in a classroom. Boring lesson, nobody is throwing chairs. Good day.
Callum: Ha! Do they throw chairs?
Agnieszka: Year 8 on a Friday, everything is possible.
Callum: Did you do the puzzle bit at the start? I was dead pleased with meself, then I got to the last one and just guessed.
Agnieszka: I did it. One question had two correct answers. Badly written.
Callum: Did it? Which one?
Agnieszka: The one with the shapes, number three. "Choose the best answer." Two were equally good.
Callum: See, that's why you'd want her on your quiz team. I run a pub quiz team on Thursdays, I'm captain. We could do with someone who argues with the quizmaster.
Agnieszka: I would argue with the quizmaster. Often he is wrong.
Callum: He is wrong! Last week he had the Moon landing as '68. Sixty-nine, mate. I've listened to about four podcasts on it.
Agnieszka: Then you were right. Did you get the point?
Callum: No! He wouldn't give it me. Still not over it.
Agnieszka: This is why I do sudoku. Nobody can tell you the answer is wrong when it is right.
Callum: That's fair, that. Erm, what do you do when you're not marking? Are you from Wakefield originally, or...?
Agnieszka: Poland. Tarnów. I came 2006. My son is seventeen, A-levels, he eats everything in the fridge. That is my hobby now, buying food for him.
Callum: Ha, me mum says the exact same about me brother. Is he going uni then?
Agnieszka: He wants to. Engineering, maybe. Like his father.
Callum: Ah, that's nice, that. Honestly I sometimes wish I'd gone. I did an apprenticeship instead, and I've no regrets, like, but I do love learning stuff. I've been looking at the company paying for an HNC, in manufacturing engineering.
Agnieszka: Then do it. If they pay, do it. You will regret it if you don't.
Callum: Yeah. Yeah, me wife says that too.
Agnieszka: Then she is also right. Two people telling you.
Callum: [laughs] Okay, okay, I'll look at the forms on—
calls.C0344:
Rebecca: Hiya! Oh, lovely, it's you. I was hoping I'd get you.
Abena: Oh, hi. Really? Sorry, I mean, hi. I'm Abena.
Rebecca: Rebecca. I'm in Exeter. How's it going so far? Have you had a call already?
Abena: Yeah, I had one. It was okay, erm, he was nice. A bit quiet. I think I talked too much about a book.
Rebecca: No such thing as too much about a book. What was it?
Abena: The Dispossessed. Ursula Le Guin.
Rebecca: Oh, I've got that! It's in the half-finished pile by my bed, which is basically a tower at this point. Is it worth getting through?
Abena: Yeah, definitely. The second half is kind of the best bit. It all comes together.
Rebecca: Right, okay, I'll dig it out. What are you studying? I saw the hoodie.
Abena: Biomedical science, first year. I'd like to go into haematology, in an NHS lab, hopefully.
Rebecca: Oh, brilliant. Why haematology?
Abena: Erm, there's sickle cell in my family, my wider family, so it's kind of always been there, you know? And I just like blood. That sounds weird.
Rebecca: Not to me it doesn't! I'm a vet, I spend half my life bleeding cows. Not in a horror film way. Taking samples, for TB testing and herd health and that sort of thing.
Abena: Oh, that's really cool. Do you do the testing yourself, or does it go to a lab?
Rebecca: Mostly off to a lab, so people like you, basically, eventually. Please be nice to my samples. They're usually a bit muddy.
Abena: [laughs] I'll try.
Rebecca: Honestly, lab people are the unsung heroes. I'm out in a freezing shed at three in the morning, knackered, guessing, and the lab are the ones who actually tell me what's going on.
Abena: My dad's a nurse, and he says the same about the lab at Broomfield. He says nobody thanks them.
Rebecca: He's right. Is he chuffed you're doing it?
Abena: Erm... yeah. I think he'd have liked medicine, kind of. But he's supportive.
Rebecca: Well, I nearly did medicine, and then I realised I liked animals more than people, mostly. You can't argue with a sheep. Well, you can, but it doesn't listen.
Abena: [laughs] Do you have pets as well, or is that too much?
Rebecca: One lurcher, Moss. That's her back end in the corner there. She stole a whole block of cheddar off the counter last week, the entire thing, wrapper and all. Proper criminal.
Abena: Oh no. Was she okay?
Rebecca: She was fine, smug, if anything. Do you have any animals?
Abena: No, not really. I've got six houseplants, and they've all got names. That's kind of it.
Rebecca: That totally counts. What are they called?
Abena: Erm, the monstera's called Gloria. She's just got a new leaf, actually, so I'm quite proud of her.
Rebecca: Gloria! That's amazing. See, you're way better at keeping things alive than me, I killed a sourdough starter. That's literally just flour and water and I couldn't—
Abena: Sorry, go on.
Rebecca: No, no, I was just going to say, Moss probably ate it.
calls.C0345:
Callum: Alright, mate! Can you hear me?
Dominic: Yeah. Hi.
Callum: I'm Callum, I'm in St Helens. You?
Dominic: Dominic. Walthamstow.
Callum: London, nice. Sorry, I've got to ask, are you on nights as well? You look about as knackered as I feel.
Dominic: [laughs] No. Just, er, a long week. I run a post-production company, so it's sort of ten till ten when it's busy.
Callum: Ten till ten, that's worse than my shifts to be fair. What's post-production, like editing and that?
Dominic: Yeah. Editing, colour grading, sound. Mostly adverts. Someone shoots it, we make it look like it was meant to look.
Callum: That's class, that. Have I seen anything you've done?
Dominic: Probably. There was a supermarket Christmas one with a fox in the snow.
Callum: No way, with the little fox? Megan, me wife, she cried at that. Proper cried.
Dominic: That was the idea, yeah. Good to know it worked on someone.
Callum: She'll be made up when I tell her. What's that print behind you? The orange one.
Dominic: Oh. Screen print, limited run, from a studio in Hackney. I haven't hung it yet. Bought it last week and I probably shouldn't have, if I'm honest.
Callum: Ha, that's how Megan talks about my running trainers. It looks good though. I'm not really arty, but I like a wander round the Walker or Tate Liverpool. I usually drag someone with me.
Dominic: Tate Liverpool's alright actually. Good building.
Callum: It's an old warehouse on the docks, isn't it? I'm more into the history bit to be fair. I listen to loads of podcasts on the drive to work, Titanic, Industrial Revolution, all that.
Dominic: What's the drive to?
Callum: The glassworks. I'm on the float line. Erm, so the molten glass comes out the furnace onto a bath of molten tin and floats flat. I'm on the hot end, so I'm checking temperatures and thickness and spotting defects before it gets anywhere near a window.
Dominic: Huh. That's sort of what a colourist does, in a way. Watching a monitor all night for the bit that's wrong.
Callum: Yeah, do you know what I mean, it's the same thing! Hours of nothing and then one little flaw and it all goes off.
Dominic: Yeah. The flaw's always on the last day, as well.
Callum: Every time. So do you get to watch much telly and films yourself, or are you sick of it?
Dominic: No, I go to the cinema a lot. On my own, mostly. Small places, the Prince Charles, the BFI. Saw a Korean thriller last week that was, er, quite good.
Callum: Quite good, or actually good?
Dominic: [laughs] Actually good. Best thing I've seen this year. It's set in one flat, basically, and by the end you're scared of the fridge.
Callum: Scared of the fridge! I'd watch that. Megan makes me watch Love Island, so anything's an upgrade, mate.
Dominic: That's a low bar.
Callum: It's on the floor. Do you follow any sport, or is it just films?
Dominic: Charlton. Because of my dad. They lost on Saturday, obviously.
Callum: Ah, I'm Saints, rugby league. Season ticket with me dad and me brother, same seats for years. It's the dads, isn't it, they get you young.
Dominic: Yeah. No way out once they've done it.
Callum: None. What's the film called anyway? I'll put it on the—
calls.C0346:
Abena: Hi. Erm, can you hear me?
Agnieszka: Yes. Hello.
Abena: Hi, I'm Abena. I'm in Chelmsford.
Agnieszka: Agnieszka. Wakefield. You are a student, yes? I can see the hoodie.
Abena: Yeah, first year, biomedical science. Sorry, I'm a bit nervous. You kind of remind me of my teachers at sixth form.
Agnieszka: I am a teacher. Maths. So you are right. But I am not marking you, so you can relax.
Abena: [laughs] Okay. That helps, actually.
Agnieszka: Biomedical. Do you have statistics?
Abena: Yeah, there's a module this term. I'm okay with it, I think. I just like to check everything like three times.
Agnieszka: Good. Check three times. Most of my students check zero times and then they are surprised.
Abena: I think I'd be one of your quiet ones. I sit at the front and I only answer if I'm sure.
Agnieszka: The quiet ones at the front are the ones who pass. The loud ones at the back, I spend my life with them. Year 8. Feral.
Abena: [laughs] My brother's fourteen, so I kind of know what you mean. He uses all the hot water and then sings in the shower.
Agnieszka: My son is seventeen. He doesn't sing, he just eats. Everything. I buy food Monday, Wednesday it is gone.
Abena: That's exactly my brother. Erm, sorry, are you from Wakefield originally?
Agnieszka: No, Poland. Tarnów, south of Poland. I came 2006, I was thirty-two.
Abena: Oh, okay. I was born in Ghana, in Kumasi. We moved here when I was six, for my dad's nursing job.
Agnieszka: Six. So you are more English than me, probably.
Abena: Kind of? I don't know. Erm, I understand Twi, but I answer my mum in English, and she teases me about it all the time.
Agnieszka: My son does the same! I speak Polish, he answers English. Every time. I ask in Polish "did you eat my cheese," and he says "no" in English.
Abena: [laughs] That's so similar.
Agnieszka: It's normal. The children are from here. We are from, I don't know. Somewhere in the middle.
Abena: Yeah. That's kind of how it feels. Like I'm not fully either. Sorry, that's quite a serious thing to say in three minutes.
Agnieszka: No, it's true. It doesn't go away. You just get used to it. I say "tea" now for the evening meal. My sister in Poland thinks I am lost.
Abena: We say dinner. My mum makes jollof on Saturdays, and honestly, hers is better than anyone's.
Agnieszka: Everyone's mother cooks the best. This is a law. What do you do when you don't study?
Abena: I read a lot. And I do botanical drawings, those on the wall.
Agnieszka: I read crime novels. Polish, Scandinavian. Somebody dies on page one, by the end the detective knows who. Simple.
Abena: I've never really read crime. What would you recommend for someone who's—
Agnieszka: Start with—
calls.C0347:
Callum: Alright! Hiya. Can you hear me okay?
Abena: Hi, yeah. Erm, I'm Abena.
Callum: Callum. I'm in St Helens, near Liverpool. Where are you?
Abena: Chelmsford. In Essex.
Callum: Ah, nice. Is that a uni hoodie? Anglia Ruskin?
Abena: Yeah, I'm in first year. Biomedical science.
Callum: Proper science, that. What's that involve, like labs and microscopes?
Abena: Yeah, kind of. We do a lot of practicals, like blood samples, cell cultures. I want to go into haematology eventually, in an NHS lab. Erm, the vet I talked to earlier said I'd be getting her muddy cow samples, so.
Callum: Ha, was that Rebecca? I've not had her yet. I'm hoping she's next, she's got a lurcher and I've got a greyhound, Dolly, so we've got loads to talk about.
Abena: Oh, Moss. She stole a block of cheese.
Callum: Did she! Dolly wouldn't, she's too scared. She's scared of the hoover, she's scared of the kettle. Honestly, thirty kilos of dog hiding behind the settee from a Dyson.
Abena: [laughs] Oh no. Bless her.
Callum: She's fine, she's spoiled rotten. What do you do when you're not studying then? I saw the plants and the drawings.
Abena: Erm, I read a lot, and I draw. Those are botanical drawings, with fine-liners. And I watch science YouTube, like explainers and stuff.
Callum: Oh, I'm the same but with podcasts. I listen on the drive to work, I'm on shifts at the glassworks. Last week I did about four hours on the Moon landings. Did you know the computer on Apollo 11 had less memory than a calculator?
Abena: Yeah, I watched a video about that! And they kept getting alarms on the way down, like error codes, and they just kind of decided to keep going.
Callum: The 1202 alarm! Yeah! That's the bit I love. Some lad in mission control, about my age, has to go, it's fine, keep going. Imagine that being your call. I get a furnace alarm on nights and I feel the pressure, and that's just glass.
Abena: That's still quite a lot of pressure though. Like, a furnace.
Callum: Yeah, to be fair, it's fifteen hundred degrees. But you just stay calm, check your readings, do what you've been trained to do. Same as them really, just less famous.
Abena: I think that's the bit I worry about. Like, in a lab, if I got something wrong with someone's blood results. I check everything three times.
Callum: Three times is good! I'm the one who logs everything at work, the older lads take the mick out of me. But it's always the tidy handover that saves you, do you know what I mean.
Abena: Yeah. That makes me feel a bit better, actually.
Callum: Good. Sorry, can I ask, is that a cross on your necklace?
Abena: Oh, yeah. Erm, I go to church. Methodist. I sing in the youth choir. I saw the crucifix on your shelf, actually, in the photo.
Callum: Ah, yeah, that was me nan's. Catholic. I'm not, like, every Sunday, I go with me mum at Christmas and Easter and the odd one. It's sort of quiet but there, if that makes sense.
Abena: No, it does. That's kind of how it is for me. Like, I don't really talk about it, but when I'm anxious, before exams and stuff, it helps.
Callum: Yeah. When me nan died last year, honestly, it was the thing that got me through. Didn't expect it to.
Abena: I'm sorry. I lost my grandma too, a few years ago. In Ghana.
Callum: Ah, sorry. It's hard, isn't it. Were you close?
Abena: Yeah, I wish I'd visited more. Sorry, that's quite heavy.
Callum: Don't be sorry. Honestly, it's better than me banging on about pub quizzes, which is what I did last call.
Abena: [laughs] Pub quizzes?
Callum: Long story. I'm captain of a team, and the quizmaster had the Moon landing as—
calls.C0348:
Rebecca: Hiya! Hello. Can you hear me?
Dominic: Yeah. Hi.
Rebecca: I'm Rebecca, Exeter. Sorry, I'm still in my work fleece, I never get changed.
Dominic: Dominic. Walthamstow. That's fine.
Rebecca: What do you do, Dominic?
Dominic: Post-production. I run a company in Soho. Editing, colour, sound, mostly adverts.
Rebecca: Oh, fancy. Anything I'd know?
Dominic: There was a fox one. Supermarket, last Christmas.
Rebecca: Oh my god, the fox! My mum sent me that about four times. She sort of, kind of sobbed at it. That's you?
Dominic: Me and about fourteen other people. But yeah.
Rebecca: That's brilliant. I'm a vet, by the way, farm animals mostly, out near Crediton. Cows, sheep, calvings at three in the morning, that kind of thing.
Dominic: Right. That's sort of the opposite of what I do.
Rebecca: How'd you mean?
Dominic: Well, nobody's going to die if a colour grade's a bit off. Clients act like it, but.
Rebecca: Ha, yeah. Although honestly, half the time it's not dying, it's just a cow being stubborn in a freezing shed and me being knackered. It's long hours. Fifty, sixty a week, and the out-of-hours on top. Which, sorry, I'm guessing you're the same? You look a bit like I feel.
Dominic: Yeah. Ten till ten when it's busy. I've been told I look tired a lot today.
Rebecca: Sorry! It wasn't a criticism. It's a club. The knackered club.
Dominic: [laughs] Fair enough.
Rebecca: Do you like it though? Like, actually like it?
Dominic: Er... yeah. Mostly. The edit suite I like. The rest is emails and invoices, and I'm not very good at those. My business partner basically holds it together.
Rebecca: Oh, that's me with clinical notes. I do them on the sofa at half ten at night, it's terrible. What do you do to switch off, if you ever do?
Dominic: Cinema. On my own, mostly. Prince Charles, the BFI. Two, three times a week when I can.
Rebecca: On your own? I love that. I've never done it. Is it nice?
Dominic: Yeah. Nobody talks to you. Nobody wants your opinion on the way out. You just sit there for two hours and nothing's your problem.
Rebecca: Nothing's your problem. God, that sounds amazing. My version is sea swimming at Exmouth. You get in, it's proper cold, and for about five minutes you can't think about anything except how cold it is. Which is kind of the same thing, I suppose, just wetter.
Dominic: I'll stick with the cinema.
Rebecca: Everyone says that. Agnieszka told me the sea's for fish.
Dominic: [laughs] I haven't had her yet.
Rebecca: Oh, you'll be fine. She's dry, but she's alright. What's the best thing you've seen lately?
Dominic: A Korean thriller, last week. All in one flat. It was alright actually.
Rebecca: "Alright actually." Is that London for brilliant?
Dominic: Pretty much.
Rebecca: Right, I'm writing it down. Do you ever get people asking you to cut their wedding videos? Because Dan's sister—
calls.C0349:
Dominic: Hi.
Agnieszka: Hello.
Dominic: Dominic. I'm in Walthamstow.
Agnieszka: Agnieszka. Wakefield.
Dominic: Rebecca said I'd get you at some point. She said you told her the sea's for fish.
Agnieszka: It is for fish. February. She swims in it. I said what I think.
Dominic: Yeah. I'm with you on that.
Agnieszka: Good. What do you do?
Dominic: I run a post-production company in Soho. Editing, colour, sound. Adverts, mostly, some TV.
Agnieszka: The fox. Callum told me. Everybody is talking about this fox.
Dominic: [laughs] It's following me round today. I've done other things, honestly.
Agnieszka: But the fox is the one people remember. This is how it is. I teach maths twenty years and the kids remember that I shouted once in 2014.
Dominic: What did you shout?
Agnieszka: "Sit down." Very loud. A boy was standing on a table. Now it's a legend at the school.
Dominic: Fair enough. That's a good legend.
Agnieszka: Mm.
Dominic: Do you like it? Teaching?
Agnieszka: The teaching, yes. Explaining something, and you see the face, they understand. That is good. The rest, no. Data drops, meetings, someone from senior leadership with a PowerPoint about "learning journeys". Twice they wanted me to be head of year. Twice I said no.
Dominic: Yeah. That's sort of me with the business side. I like the edit suite. The spreadsheets I leave to my business partner. If it was up to me we'd have gone bust in about a week.
Agnieszka: At least you know. Most people in management don't know.
Dominic: [laughs] I'll take that.
Agnieszka: What do you do when you are not working? You look like you are always working.
Dominic: That's the third time someone's said that today. Er, cinema, mostly. On my own. Small cinemas. I saw a Korean thriller last week that was, er, quite good.
Agnieszka: Thriller. With a detective?
Dominic: Sort of. There's a police officer, but he's useless, which is the point. It's more about this family in one flat, and something's wrong with the neighbour, and you spend two hours not sure who's lying. By the end you don't trust anyone in it, including the kid. It's very tight. Nothing wasted. Every shot's doing a job.
Agnieszka: I like this. I read crime novels, Polish and Scandinavian. And I watch every detective series on the TV. My husband used to say I always know who did it by twenty minutes.
Dominic: Do you?
Agnieszka: Usually. In British dramas, it's the famous actor who is in the first episode for only one scene. Always him.
Dominic: [laughs] Yeah. That's a casting problem. Once you've paid for someone, you have to use them.
Agnieszka: So I am right.
Dominic: You're right. Don't tell anyone in the industry.
Agnieszka: I don't know anyone in the industry. Only you.
Dominic: Then it's safe.
Agnieszka: You go to galleries also? You have this print behind you, the orange.
Dominic: Yeah, a bit. Openings, studios in East London. I haven't hung that one yet.
Agnieszka: In Wakefield we have the Hepworth. I went once when it opened. A lot of concrete.
Dominic: It is a lot of concrete. I've been, actually. The building's alright. Some of the Hepworth pieces are, er, very good.
Agnieszka: Maybe. I looked at the concrete, I looked at the river, I went home.
Dominic: That's a review, to be fair.
Agnieszka: Short reviews are best. Like my marking. "Show working." Done.
Dominic: What's the Polish crime writer I should read? If I was going to start somewhere.
Agnieszka: Somewhere easy, translated. There is one, Miłoszewski, the prosecutor Szacki books. He is miserable, everybody is miserable, it rains. You would like it.
Dominic: Why would I—
Agnieszka: Because you look like you would like miserable people in the rain. I mean it nicely.

C0348.line_text: Nobody talks to you. Nobody wants your opinion on the way out. You just sit there for two hours and nothing's your problem.
C0348.what: In the bottom right corner of Rebecca's frame, the brindle lurcher climbs out of the grey dog bed, stretches, and walks across behind Rebecca's chair and out of shot to the left. Rebecca doesn't turn round.
